title: Proof of Payment When You Pay Vendors Manually
summary: Approved is not paid. How finance teams that pay vendors manually across several banks capture proof of payment, post at the right time and notify suppliers.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Many finance teams pay vendors manually on purpose because money moves through several banks, wallets, cards and an ERP that already handles payments. That choice is reasonable, but it creates a gap: a bill can be approved for payment without anyone proving it was paid. Closing that gap takes six controls: separate bill approval from payment release, record the payment rail, require proof of payment before a payment is marked complete, post the ledger entry only when evidence exists, send payment advice to the vendor automatically, and reconcile every evidenced payment against the bank feed with an age clock on anything still unproven.


## Introduction


Ask a finance director whether a bill has been paid and the honest answer is often a question back: approved, or actually paid?


With one automated payment rail, those are the same thing. When vendors are paid from several banks, a wallet, corporate cards and auto-debits, they are not: the bill is approved in one system and paid somewhere else, by a person, on a day nobody records.


This guide draws on conversations with multi-entity finance teams in Southeast Asia that process a few hundred bills a month, approve payments in two layers and have chosen not to route every payment through one automated account. The aim is to make manual payment as controlled and auditable as automated payment.


## What Is Proof of Payment?


**Proof of payment is the evidence that money actually left your account for a specific vendor bill.** It typically takes the form of a bank transfer confirmation, a downloadable payment slip from an internet banking portal, a card transaction receipt, or the matching line on a bank statement. A usable proof shows the date, amount, currency, payee and a transaction reference.


It is related to, but not the same as, **payment advice** . Payment advice is the message you send to the supplier telling them a payment has been made and which invoices it covers. Proof of payment is what you keep. Payment advice is what you send, ideally with the proof attached.


For[accounts payable](https://peakflo.co/accounts-payable) , proof of payment is the hinge between three records that otherwise drift apart: the approved bill, the ledger payment entry and the bank statement.


## Why Do Finance Teams Still Pay Vendors Manually?


It is tempting to treat manual payment as a legacy habit. In practice, the teams we speak with have specific, defensible reasons.


Reason for manual payment What it looks like in practice Why it is rational


Several payment rails Vendors paid from two or three banks, a wallet, cards and auto-debits No single integration covers every rail


ERP already pays for one entity The higher-volume entity’s ERP has its own bank payment flow Rebuilding a working process adds risk


No appetite for another funded account Automated payouts require pre-funding a dedicated account One more balance to monitor and reconcile


FX preferences Existing banks offer known rates on foreign currency payments Switching rails changes FX cost unpredictably


Senior sign-off in the bank CEO or senior management releases payments directly in the bank portal Authority sits where the money sits


Each is a legitimate trade-off. The problem is that most AP processes assume the system that approves a bill also pays it. When that breaks, nobody owns the step in between.


Our guide to[the last mile problem in AP](https://peakflo.co/blog/treasury-finops-manual-payment-execution-ap-automation-last-mile) makes the case for automating execution where you can. This article deals with what to do where you cannot, or choose not to.


## Where Does the Manual Payment Loop Break?


There are four distinct failure points, and they compound. A released bill sits in an approved state while the person meant to execute it is on leave or busy with month-end. The AP system posts the payment entry at approval, so the ledger shows cash leaving before it has. The vendor is never told and emails to ask. And even when the ledger entry and the bank line both exist, someone still matches them by hand because the references do not obviously relate.


Failure point Visible symptom Typical discovery Business impact


Approved but not executed Vendor chases a payment you believe was made Supplier email or call Late fees, strained supplier relationships


Posted on approval Ledger cash and bank cash disagree Bank reconciliation Rework, reversals, misleading cash reports


No payment advice Repeated where-is-my-payment queries Inbox volume Finance hours lost to manual forwarding


Manual bank matching Unreconciled items pile up Month-end close Slower close, audit queries


Bodies such as the[Association for Financial Professionals](https://www.afponline.org/) consistently identify payment exceptions and supplier inquiries as major hidden drivers of AP cost. Most of those exceptions trace back to one of the four failure points above.


## Bill Approval and Payment Approval Are Two Different Decisions


Many of the teams we speak with already run two layers of approval. Business owners approve the bill based on rules such as amount, vendor category and budget category. A second layer, often the CEO or senior management, decides whether and when to actually pay it.


That is good control design, and it aligns with the principle of[segregation of duties in accounts payable](https://peakflo.co/blog/segregation-of-duties-accounts-payable-internal-controls) . But it is only half the design. The bill approver confirms the bill is valid. The payment approver confirms the business is willing to release cash. Neither confirms that cash was actually released.


A complete design has three distinct states after a bill is captured:


State Who acts What it proves What it does not prove


Bill approved Budget or category owner The bill is valid and correctly coded That it should be paid now


Payment released Payment approver (for example CEO) The business has authorised the cash outflow That anyone executed the transfer


Payment evidenced Person who executed the transfer Money has left the account, with a reference Nothing further needed, apart from bank matching


A useful refinement that finance leaders often adopt is to make the person who uploads the payment slip act as the final confirmer. They are the one person who knows for certain the transfer happened, so their upload becomes the event that closes the payment.


The[COSO internal control framework](https://www.coso.org/) describes exactly this kind of control activity: an independent piece of evidence confirming that an authorised transaction was executed as authorised.


## When Should a Manual Payment Be Posted to the Ledger?


This is the question that causes the most confusion in implementations, and there are three common answers.


The three options below differ in when the ledger entry is created: at approval, when proof is uploaded, or inside an ERP that already executes bank payments for that entity.


Posting option Best suited to Main risk Mitigation


A: Post on approval Fast, controlled execution on the same day Ledger shows unpaid bills as paid Daily check of released versus executed


B: Post on proof upload Manual payments across several banks or wallets Executor forgets to upload Age clock and escalation on unevidenced payments


C: Hand off to ERP payments Entities where the ERP already pays the bank Two systems with partial views Sync payment status back for visibility


In multi-entity groups it is common to use different options in different entities. That is fine, provided each entity’s rule is documented and consistent. Our article on[integration-agnostic AP automation across mixed ERP estates](https://peakflo.co/blog/integration-agnostic-ap-automation-mixed-erp-estates) explains how to run one payables process even when the downstream systems differ.


## How to Build a Proof of Payment Loop: Six Steps


**Step 1: Separate the bill decision from the payment decision.** Configure two approval stages with different owners. A bill that passes the first stage moves into a queue for the payment approver rather than straight into a paid state.


**Step 2: Record the payment rail at release.** When the payment approver releases a bill, capture which bank account, wallet or card will be used. This tells the executor where to pay and tells the reconciler which bank feed to check.


**Step 3: Make proof of payment a required upload.** The bill cannot move to paid until the executor attaches the bank confirmation or payment slip. Mobile upload matters here because many executors approve and pay from their phones.


**Step 4: Post the payment entry only after evidence exists.** For manual rails, create the ledger payment entry from the uploaded evidence, using the actual payment date and debited amount.


**Step 5: Send payment advice to the vendor automatically.** The moment proof is attached, email the vendor contact a payment advice listing the invoices covered, with the proof attached. Provide a manual resend option for vendors who ask again or whose contact has changed.


**Step 6: Reconcile against the bank feed and chase gaps.** Match each evidenced payment to its bank statement line. Report every bill that has been released but not evidenced, with the number of days it has been waiting, and escalate beyond a threshold.


```text
Bill captured
-> Bill approved (category / amount / budget rules)
-> Payment released (payment approver, rail recorded)
-> Transfer executed offline (bank portal, wallet or card)
-> Proof uploaded (executor) -> Payment entry posted to ledger
-> Payment advice emailed to vendor with proof attached
-> Matched to bank feed line
Exception: released but no proof after N days -> escalate
```


## What Should a Proof of Payment Record Contain?


A photo of a banking app screen is better than nothing, but a proper record makes reconciliation, audit and vendor queries trivial.


Field Why it matters Where it comes from


Payment date Drives the ledger posting date and aging Bank confirmation


Amount and currency debited Supports FX difference calculation Bank confirmation or statement


Payer bank account Tells the reconciler which feed to match Recorded at release


Payee name and bank details Confirms the right vendor was paid Bank confirmation


Bank transaction reference Enables automated bank matching Bank confirmation


Bills covered Lets the vendor apply cash correctly AP system


Executor Accountability and audit trail User who uploaded the proof


Storing the proof against the bill, rather than in an email thread or shared drive, also simplifies audits. Auditors increasingly expect a direct link from ledger entry to source evidence, which is a theme the[Institute of Management Accountants](https://www.imanet.org/) highlights in its guidance on finance process documentation.


## What About Multi-Currency and FX Payments?


Manual payment across several banks is often driven by currency, which makes evidence more important. At approval, a foreign currency bill is valued at an assumed rate. At execution, the bank debits an actual base-currency amount. Posting from the proof captures that actual amount, so the realised FX difference is booked from evidence, consistent with the[IFRS Foundation](https://www.ifrs.org/) distinction between transaction-date and settlement-date amounts. Track released but unevidenced bills and vendor payment queries monthly; both should fall towards zero once the loop is in place, a measurement discipline[IFAC](https://www.ifac.org/) recommends for every finance hand-off.

Peakflo’s[payment automation](https://peakflo.co/accounts-payable/payment-automation) is designed so that teams do not have to choose one model for every vendor and entity.


- **Two-stage approvals.** Bill approvals route by amount, vendor category and budget category through[approval workflow automation](https://peakflo.co/accounts-payable/approval-workflow-automation) . Payment release is a separate approval that can sit with the CEO or senior management.

## Our Verdict: Should You Formalise Proof of Payment or Automate Payments Outright?


After working through this pattern with multi-entity finance teams, our view is that the two are not alternatives. Proof of payment controls are worth formalising regardless of how payments are executed.


### Formalise a proof of payment loop now if


- You pay vendors from more than one bank, wallet or card
- One or more entities already pay through an ERP’s own bank flow
- Payment release sits with the CEO or senior management in the bank portal
- Vendors regularly email to ask whether they have been paid
- Bank reconciliation regularly surfaces payments posted on the wrong date


### Consider automated payouts as well if


- Most vendors are paid in currencies and corridors one platform covers well
- You are comfortable maintaining a funded payout account
- Payment volume is high enough that manual execution consumes meaningful time each week


**Our Recommendation** : Treat approved, released and evidenced as three separate states, post manual payments from evidence rather than from approval, and let the system send payment advice automatically. That removes most of the risk of manual payment while keeping the flexibility that made you choose it. Automate execution later, rail by rail, where the economics are clear.


## Conclusion


Manual vendor payment is not a failure of automation. For many growing, multi-entity businesses it is a sensible response to several banks, several currencies and senior sign-off that lives in the bank portal. What makes it risky is the unowned gap between approval and execution.


Close that gap with evidence. Require proof of payment before a bill is marked paid, post the ledger entry from that evidence, send the vendor a payment advice with the proof attached, and reconcile every evidenced payment against the bank feed. Your ledger will match your bank, your suppliers will stop chasing and your auditors will find every payment linked to its source.

## Frequently Asked Questions


**What is proof of payment in accounts payable?** Proof of payment is the evidence that money actually left your account for a specific vendor bill. It is usually a bank transfer confirmation, a payment slip, a card receipt or a bank statement line that shows the date, amount, payee and a reference.


**What is the difference between proof of payment and payment advice?** Proof of payment is the evidence you hold that a transfer happened. Payment advice is the notification you send to the supplier telling them which invoices a payment covers. Good practice attaches the proof to the advice so the vendor can apply the cash without calling you.


**Why is an approved bill not the same as a paid bill?** Approval is a decision that a bill is valid and may be paid. Payment is an action someone must still execute in a bank portal, wallet or card platform. When payments are executed manually, the gap between the two is where missed and duplicate payments occur.


**When should the payment entry be posted to the ledger for a manual payment?** Post the payment entry when evidence of execution exists, not at the moment of approval. Posting on approval risks showing a bill as paid in the ledger while the transfer has not happened yet, which distorts cash and aging reports.


**Why do some companies keep paying vendors manually instead of automating payments?** Common reasons include paying from several banks and wallets, an ERP that already handles bank payments for one entity, reluctance to fund and manage an extra payment account, FX preferences with existing banks and approval rules that require senior sign-off in the bank portal itself.


**What should a proof of payment record contain?** At minimum the payment date, amount and currency, payer bank account, payee name and bank details, the bank transaction reference, the bills covered and the name of the person who executed the transfer.


**How do you notify a vendor after paying them manually?** Upload the bank confirmation against the bill in your AP system and let it send a payment advice email to the vendor contact automatically, listing the invoices paid and attaching the proof. Keep a manual resend option for vendors who ask again.


**How do you catch payments that were approved but never executed?** Track every bill in a released but unevidenced state with an age clock. Any bill that stays there beyond an agreed number of days is escalated to the executor and the payment approver before the vendor chases.


**Can bank reconciliation be automated if payments are made manually?** Yes. As long as the payment entry in the ledger carries the correct amount, date and reference, it can be matched to the bank feed line automatically or with one click, even though the transfer itself was executed by a person.


**Does this approach work for FX payments?** Yes, and it matters more for FX. The proof of payment captures the actual amount debited in base currency, so the realised exchange difference can be booked from evidence rather than from the rate assumed at approval.
